headline: Giri is from Middle Chinese 義理, which first meant “righteous principle” and narrowed in Japan during the Muromachi and Edo periods.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 義理 (MC ngjeH liX).

Originally, in Middle Chinese and early Japanese attestations, the term carried a philosophical and textual meaning of “righteous principle”, “reason”, or “significance”. During the Muromachi and Edo periods, under the influence of a stratified feudal society, samurai ethics, and the merchant class, the concept underwent semantic narrowing in Japan. The “correct path” shifted to refer specifically to the reciprocal behavioral norms, social debts, and favors expected between individuals in a hierarchical community. This transformed the philosophical concept into a localized social contract and “burden of obligation”, famously contrasting with 人情 (ninjō, “human feeling”). This specialized sense developed entirely internally within Japan.

examples.ja: 私は彼に義理を立てなければならない。
examples.en: I have to do right by him.

examples.ja: 日本語の「義理」に相当する英語は見つからない。
examples.en: We cannot find an English equivalent for the Japanese 'giri'.

headline: Hitojichi is 人 (hito, “person”) plus 質 (shichi, “pawn, hock”), and first meant “indentureship”, with “hostage” arising by extension.

sources.quote: Compound of 人 (hito, “person”) + 質 (shichi, “pawn, hock”). The shichi changes to jichi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

The original sense was “indentureship”, from the sense of a person being as if in pawn until a debt is paid. The “hostage” sense then arose by extension, from the person being in pawn until a ransom is paid or some other condition is met.

examples.ja: 人質は解放されるだろう。
examples.en: The hostages will be released.

examples.ja: 人質は無事全員解放された。
examples.en: All the hostages were released unharmed.

headline: Ninmei is from Middle Chinese 任命, “burden, charge + command”.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese compound 任命 (MC nyimH mjaengH, “burden, charge + command”). Compare modern Mandarin 任命 (rènmìng, “to appoint”).

examples.ja: 彼は議長に任命された。
examples.en: He was appointed chairman.

headline: Kakageru is a regular shift from Classical Japanese 掲ぐ (kakagu), itself a contraction of 掻き上ぐ (kakiagu).

sources.quote: A regular shift from Classical Japanese 掲(かか)ぐ (kakagu), itself a contraction of 掻(か)き上(あ)ぐ (kakiagu, modern form 掻(か)き上(あ)げる (kakiageru)).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

examples.ja: 彼は旗をかかげた。
examples.en: He put up a flag.

examples.ja: 以下に掲げる人が合格です。
examples.en: The following persons passed the examination.

sources.quote: 発 is a daiyōji replacing 撥.

examples.ja: 若者達は本来、親の考えに対して反発するものだ。
examples.en: It is quite natural for young people to rebel against their parents.

examples.en: In the financial world opposition is apparently increasing against the withdrawal of the proposed bill.

headline: Ryōshō is 了 (ryō, “comprehend”) plus 承 (shō, “agree to”), and 了 is a daiyōji replacing 諒.

sources.quote: From 了 (ryō, “comprehend”) + 承 (shō, “agree to”). 了 (“to finish”) is a daiyōji replacing 諒 (“to excuse, to forgive; to guess, to presume”).

examples.ja: この件についてのあなたのお求めを了承します。
examples.en: Your request of this matter has been accepted.

headline: Otozureru is from the Classical Japanese verb otoduru, analysable as 音 (oto, “sound”) plus 連れる (tsureru, “to bring along; to accompany”), with rendaku.

sources.quote: From Classical Japanese verb 訪(おとづ)る (otoduru). Analyzable as 音(おと) (oto, “sound”) + 連(つ)れる (tsureru, “to bring along; to accompany”); the tsureru changes to zureru as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

examples.ja: 人間がすべての石油を使い切ってしまうときがおとずれるかもしれない。
examples.en: The time may come when people will have used up all the oil.

headline: Masashiku is the adverbial form of the classical adjective 正し (masashi).

sources.quote: Adverbial form of 正(まさ)し (masashi, classical adjective).

sources.quote: 投(な)げる (nageru, “to throw”) + 出(だ)す (dasu, “to send out”)
